title: Meerkats travel in packs. But they also make great solo navigators, researchers have found
summary: When it comes to animals that travel in groups, like meerkats, it can be hard to tell how much they're navigating based on collective wisdom versus individual knowledge. So researchers separated…

image.caption: Researchers put GPS collars on meerkats at the Kalahari Research Centre in South Africa, separated them from their clans, and tracked them as they navigated their way home. (Mathilde Martin)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

When it comes to animals that travel in groups, like meerkats, it can be hard to tell how much they're navigating based on collective wisdom versus individual knowledge. So researchers separated meerkats from their clans to see if they could find their way home.
Separated from their clans, most meerkats journeyed 1.5 kilometres to find their way home
Don't let Disney's The Lion King fool you. Meerkats don't hang out with warthogs, and they have plenty of worries — like finding enough delicious grubs to eat and fending off predators.
But the African critters handle whatever life throws at them by working together. They burrow together, raise their babies together and forage for food together.

Because of their co-operative nature, scientists figured they also relied on each other, to some degree, to navigate their terrain, with the more experienced travellers mapping the area and guiding the others.
But it turns out that most meerkats, when separated from their group, can find their way home all by themselves.

"They were very good at navigating," said University of Zurich biologist Mathilde Martin, lead author of a new study into meerkat solo navigation published in the Journal of Experimental Biology. "It was surprising."
Initial confusion

Meerkats are members of the mongoose family who live in groups of roughly 30 to 50 known as clans or mobs. They live in southern Africa, primarily in arid climates like deserts, savannas and grasslands.
Clanmates are rarely apart — that is, until Martin and her colleagues came along.

The researchers put GPS collars on 20 meerkats from five clans at the Kalahari Research Centre in South Africa. Then, one at a time, they gently scooped up the collared critters, put them in bags and released them 1.5 kilometres from their burrows.
Most of the meerkats made it back on their home without assistance. (Submitted by Mathilde Martin)
At first, Martin says, the relocated meerkats were confused.
"They needed a bit of time to calm down and think about what happened to them," she told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.
But once they got their wits about them, she says, they explored their new surroundings and charted a course home.
"When they started committing to a direction, they were very good at navigating," she said.
Eighteen of the meerkats made it home and reunited with their clans, she said, while two remained frozen in place.
"For ethical obvious reasons, we didn't want them to stay away from their group for too long," Martin said. "So after 90 minutes, we took them back to the group."
Males aren't necessarily better navigators, study finds
So why abduct innocent meerkats and separate them from their clans?
When it comes to animals who live collectively, the study says it can be hard to distinguish between group wisdom and individual knowledge.
The purpose of the study was to "disentangle what individuals know on their own from how such information is incorporated into collective movement decisions."
Researchers didn't find any difference between age and sex when it came to meerkats' ability to navigate solo. (Submitted by Mathilde Martin)
Martin says she expected adult males to make better navigators because of their tendency to go "roving."
"Some time during their life, [they] leave the group and seek for mating opportunities," she said. "And, so, they do solo navigation in their natural environment without those experiments."
Females, by contrast, "usually stay with their group their whole life," she said.
But, in the experiment, the females didn't spend any longer than the males exploring their drop-off point before heading in the right direction.
"We thought maybe they were a bit less good at navigating on their own, because they don't need to learn this and they could rely on their group," Martin said. "But they were great."
Pregnant females can get expelled from clan
Christine Drea, who has studied meerkat reproduction strategies, wasn't surprised. She says female meerkats aren't always so tight-knit.
Meerkat clans, she says, tend to have a dominant female who doesn't want her offspring to have any competition when it comes to collective babysitting.
"Usually, when a subordinate gets pregnant, she represents a threat," said Drea, a Duke University anthropologist who wasn't involved in the navigation study.
"And then the dominant female targets her for aggression until she's expelled from the group. She's basically sent off to the gulag."
Pregnant meerkats, she says, don't fare well on their own.
"She can't raise them by herself and feed herself, so her young are doomed to die," Drea said. "And once they die, once she's no longer pregnant, she also can go back to the clan."

blocks.text: Still, the study notes, when females are expelled they remain just outside the periphery of the clan, while males roam farther from home.
The study also found no difference in navigational skills based on age. Even younger meerkats who had no prior roaming or expulsion experience made it home.
How they did it, Martin says, remains to be discovered. But she's glad her research is spreading some knowledge of meerkats beyond what can be gleaned from Timon and Pumba.
"The picture we have of meerkat is this mongoose in The Lion King that is a solitary individual that doesn't live with a group and other individuals. And that's very wrong," Martin said.
